## neuvector
NeuVector container security control plane.

Read before acting:
- Resolve objects before operating on them. Workload ids come from
  nv_list_workloads; group names from nv_list_groups; registry names from
  nv_list_registries. Never guess an id.
- Every mutating tool is a two-step handshake. Call it once WITHOUT 'confirm' to
  get a plan describing the exact effect plus a confirm token, then call again
  with that token. A plan is not a change; nothing was sent to the controller.
- Policy mode meanings: Discover learns and allows, Monitor alerts only, Protect
  blocks. Moving a group to Protect can break a running application.
- Vulnerability and event queries can return very large result sets. Filter by
  namespace, severity or time window first, then page with 'start'.
- When a tool reports truncated=true, either narrow the filter or page; do not
  assume the returned set is complete.

# Fewer Permission Prompts

Look through my transcripts' MCP and bash tool calls, and based on those, make a prioritized list of patterns that I should add to my permission allowlist to reduce permission prompts. Focus on read-only commands.

The format for permissions is: `Bash(foo*)`, `Bash(foo)`, `Bash(foo bar *)`, `mcp__slack__slack_read_thread`, etc.

Then, add these to the project `.claude/settings.json` under `permissions.allow`.

## Steps

1. **Locate transcripts.** Session transcripts live at `~/.claude/projects/<sanitized-cwd>/*.jsonl`. Each line is a JSON object. Tool calls appear as `assistant` messages with `message.content[]` entries of `type: "tool_use"`. The `name` field identifies the tool (e.g. `"Bash"`, `"mcp__slack__slack_read_thread"`); for Bash, `input.command` is the shell string.

   Scan the recent transcripts across the user's projects dir — not just the current project — so the allowlist reflects their actual usage. Cap the scan at a reasonable number of recent sessions (e.g. 50 most-recently-modified JSONL files) so this stays fast.

2. **Extract tool-call frequencies.**
   - For `Bash` calls: parse `input.command`, take the leading command token (handling `sudo`, `timeout`, pipes, `&&`, env-var prefixes). Record the command + first subcommand pair (e.g. `git status`, `gh pr view`, `ls`, `cat`).
   - For MCP calls: record the full tool name (e.g. `mcp__slack__slack_read_thread`).
   - Count occurrences across the scanned transcripts.

3. **Filter to read-only.** Keep only commands that don't mutate state. Examples of read-only: `ls`, `cat`, `pwd`, `git status`, `git log`, `git diff`, `git show`, `git branch`, `rg`, `grep`, `find`, `head`, `tail`, `wc`, `file`, `which`, `echo`, `date`, `gh pr view`, `gh pr list`, `gh pr diff`, `gh issue view`, `gh issue list`, `gh run list`, `gh run view`, `gh api` (GET), `bun run typecheck`, `bun run lint`, `bun run test` (for tests that don't mutate), `docker ps`, `docker logs`, `kubectl get`, `kubectl describe`, `ps`, `top`, `df`, `du`, `env`, `printenv`, any MCP tool with `read`/`get`/`list`/`search`/`view` in its name.

   Drop anything that writes, deletes, renames, pushes, merges, installs, or runs a build/test that has side effects. When in doubt, leave it out.

   **Never allowlist a pattern that grants arbitrary code execution.** A wildcard rule for any of these (e.g. `Bash(python3:*)`) is equivalent to allowing arbitrary code execution. This list is not exhaustive — apply the same rule to anything in the same category:
   - Interpreters: `python`/`python3`, `node`, `bun`, `deno`, `ruby`, `perl`, `php`, `lua`, etc.
   - Shells: `bash`, `sh`, `zsh`, `fish`, `eval`, `exec`, `ssh`, etc.
   - Package runners: `npx`, `bunx`, `uvx`, `uv run`, etc.

   - `gh api *`, `docker run`/`exec`, `kubectl exec`, `sudo`, and similar

   - **Always auto-allowed (any args):** `cal`, `uptime`, `cat`, `head`, `tail`, `wc`, `stat`, `strings`, `hexdump`, `od`, `nl`, `id`, `uname`, `free`, `df`, `du`, `locale`, `groups`, `nproc`, `basename`, `dirname`, `realpath`, `cut`, `paste`, `tr`, `column`, `tac`, `rev`, `fold`, `expand`, `unexpand`, `fmt`, `comm`, `cmp`, `numfmt`, `readlink`, `diff`, `true`, `false`, `sleep`, `which`, `type`, `expr`, `seq`, `tsort`, `pr`, `echo`, `ls`, `cd`.
   - **Auto-allowed with zero args only:** `pwd`, `whoami`, `alias`.
   - **Auto-allowed exact forms:** `claude -h`, `claude --help`, `node -v`, `node --version`, `python --version`, `python3 --version`, `ip addr`.
   - **Auto-allowed with safe flags only (validated):** `xargs`, `file`, `sed` (read-only expressions), `sort`, `man`, `help`, `netstat`, `ps`, `base64`, `grep`, `egrep`, `fgrep`, `sha256sum`, `sha1sum`, `md5sum`, `tree`, `date`, `hostname`, `lsof`, `pgrep`, `tput`, `ss`, `fd`, `fdfind`, `aki`, `rg`, `jq`, `uniq`, `history`, `arch`, `ifconfig`, `pyright`, `find` (blocks `-delete`/`-exec`/`-execdir`/`-ok`/`-okdir`/`-fprint*`/`-fls`/`-files0-from`), `printf` (blocks any `-flag`), `test` (blocks `-v`/`-R`/`-a`/`-o`).
   - **All git read-only subcommands:** `git status`, `git log`, `git diff`, `git show`, `git blame`, `git branch`, `git tag`, `git remote`, `git ls-files`, `git ls-remote`, `git config --get`, `git rev-parse`, `git describe`, `git stash list`, `git reflog`, `git shortlog`, `git cat-file`, `git for-each-ref`, `git worktree list`, etc.

   - **Docker read-only subcommands:** `docker ps`, `docker images`, `docker logs`, `docker inspect`.

   Source of truth: `src/tools/BashTool/readOnlyValidation.ts` (`READONLY_COMMANDS`, `READONLY_NOARGS`, `READONLY_EXACT`, `COMMAND_ALLOWLIST`) and `src/utils/shell/readOnlyCommandValidation.ts` (`GIT_READ_ONLY_COMMANDS`, `GH_READ_ONLY_COMMANDS`, `DOCKER_READ_ONLY_COMMANDS`, `RIPGREP_READ_ONLY_COMMANDS`, `PYRIGHT_READ_ONLY_COMMANDS`). @classmethod
    def from_api(cls, raw: dict[str, Any]) -> WorkloadBrief:
        """Project a ``RESTWorkload``/``RESTWorkloadV2`` item.

        v2 splits one workload across three places: identity under ``brief``,
        policy and vulnerability counts under ``security``, and ``running`` at
        the item's top level. Flat payloads keep everything at the top level, so
        each section falls back to ``raw``.
        """
        brief = raw.get("brief") or raw.get("workload_brief") or raw
        security = raw.get("security") or raw
        scan = security.get("scan_summary") or brief.get("scan_summary") or {}
        return cls(
            id=str(brief.get("id", "")),
            name=str(brief.get("name", "")),
            namespace=str(brief.get("domain", "") or ""),
            service=str(brief.get("service", "") or ""),
            image=str(brief.get("image", "") or ""),
            state=str(brief.get("state", "") or ""),
            policy_mode=str(security.get("policy_mode", "") or ""),  # type: ignore[arg-type]
            high_vuls=int(scan.get("high") or brief.get("high") or 0),
            med_vuls=int(scan.get("medium") or brief.get("medium") or 0),
            host_name=str(brief.get("host_name", "") or ""),

All five of the handoff's next-steps are done. Summary:

## Root cause

The handoff was right to insist on measuring — the obvious `workload_brief` nesting was wrong on **two** counts. The real v2 item splits one workload across three places:

```
{ "brief":    { id, name, display_name, domain, service, image, state, host_name },
  "security": { policy_mode, scan_summary: { high, medium, critical } },
  "running":  true/false          ← item top level
}
```

The key is **`brief`**, not `workload_brief` — so `raw.get("workload_brief")` returned `None`, `brief` fell back to `raw`, and every lookup missed. `running` was the sole survivor because it is the only projected field that genuinely lives at the item root. That's the detail the handoff flagged as "the whole puzzle," and it's now fully accounted for: `policy_mode` and the vuln counts were *also* misplaced (under `security`), which the old code read from `brief`.

## The fix

`WorkloadBrief.from_api` (`src/neuvector_mcp/models.py:61`) now resolves three sections independently, each falling back to `raw` so flat payloads still work:

```python
brief    = raw.get("brief") or raw.get("workload_brief") or raw
security = raw.get("security") or raw
scan     = security.get("scan_summary") or brief.get("scan_summary") or {}
```

`nv_get_workload` **did** share the bug — `GET /v2/workload/{id}` returns the identical nested item under a `workload` key. It's fixed by the same change. `compliance_workload.json` is a bench report and never touched this projection, so that part of the audit is clear.

## Verification

- Captured the real controller payload from inside the deployed pod — no source patching, no local credential handling, so there was no temporary dump to remove.
- Projected 6 **live** workloads through the fixed code: all fields populate, **0 items with an empty id**, and the `48/54` vuln counts and `exit` vs `discover` states come through correctly.
- `make verify`: **433 passed, 1 xfailed, 97.16% coverage, R1–R9 clean.**
- Fixtures: `workloads_v2.json` rebuilt from the real nested shape (redacted); new `workloads_flat.json` preserves the flat case. Three new tests cover the nested branch, the flat branch, and `nv_get_workload` — the branch the handoff noted had **zero** coverage.

## Two things worth your call

- **I kept `name` as `brief.name`** (`k8s_POD_api-…_prod_…`) rather than the prettier `brief.display_name`. Reason: `name_prefix` filters server-side on `f_name`, so projecting `display_name` would have users filtering on a string they can't see. Adding `display_name` as a separate field is a clean follow-up if you want the readable name.
- **`scan_summary.critical` exists but the model has no `critical_vuls` field** — only high/medium. Live data shows non-zero criticals. Out of scope for this bug; flagging it.

`uv.lock` shows one line changed — the lock catching up to pyproject's already-bumped `1.0.2`. Legitimate, belongs with the commit.

The deployed pod still runs the buggy 1.0.2 image, so `nv_list_workloads` over MCP will keep returning empty rows until a rebuild. Want me to commit this first, or go straight to rebuilding and redeploying so we can confirm end-to-end over MCP before the queued `/fossa-protect` re-run?

Fix empty workload fields by reading the v2 nested sections

nv_list_workloads returned rows whose every string field was empty while
`running` alone varied correctly true/false. `running` was the sole
survivor because it is the only projected field that lives at the item's
top level.

The v2 controller splits one workload across three places:

  brief     id, name, domain, service, image, state, host_name
  security  policy_mode, scan_summary.{high,medium}
  <root>    running

WorkloadBrief.from_api read the nesting key as `workload_brief`, but the
controller sends `brief`. The lookup missed, `brief` fell back to the item
root, and every field but `running` came back empty. policy_mode and the
vulnerability counts were doubly misplaced: they live under `security`,
not in the brief at all.

Each section now resolves independently and falls back to the item root,
so flat payloads keep working.

nv_get_workload shared the bug -- GET /v2/workload/{id} returns the same
nested item under a `workload` key -- and is fixed by the same change.

Verified against a live controller: six real workloads project with every
field populated and no empty ids.

The old workloads_v2.json fixture was flat, so the nested branch had zero
coverage and the suite could not catch this. It is replaced with a fixture
derived from a real (redacted) payload; workloads_flat.json preserves the
flat case so both branches stay covered.
